newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH - Labor silent on unemployment solution.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH - Labor silent on unemployment solution.

text.p: No-one seems to have stopped to think about it, but the 8.4 percent trough that emerged in the unemployment rate last year was by far the worst development in recent Australian economic history.
But the Labor opposition really has had very little to say on the issue.
Somehow it has focussed political attention on the peripheral issue of setting an unemployment goal without substantially addressing the question of how lower unemployment might be achieved.

The unemployment rate goes up and down with the business cycle, but each peak tends to be higher than the previous peak and while successive troughs are higher than the previous trough. (See the table at the foot of this report.)
And now it seems the economy cannot get the rate below 8.4 percent, the trend-series low recorded from May 1995 to January 1996, after which it began rising again.
It is a mystery that the country is not in uproar over this. Perhaps everyone is just so inured to it. But the issue here is: what exactly is Labor's solution?
We know what its solution was when it was in government -- microeconomic reform to push the economy faster, reinforced with retraining in labour market programmes.

As Labor sprints relentlessly to the left, differentiating itself as far as possible from the Liberal-National government, it no longer utters a word of support for the sort of painful attacks on inefficiency that motivated it for 13 years.
It still backs the labour market programmes, which the government cut back drastically in the August budget.
But reform and all its works have become dangerous right-wing ideology, according to the opposition.
The nearest solution to unemployment is opposition treasury spokesman Gareth Evans's Keynesian suggestion that smaller budget cuts would make the economy run faster.

If true, that would produce some extra jobs, but of course the Reserve Bank can make the economy run as fast as it wants by adjusting the monetary lever. The issue is how fast can Australia afford to run its economy.
Perhaps Labor's biggest problem is that the labour market stalled while it was in power -- about a year before the March 1996 election, in fact.
That suggests that even the lower degree of economic reform that it used to advocate was inadequate.
